1.note: The psalmist uses the word **Surely** to emphasize the truth of what follows. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation or use a natural form in your language for expressing this emphasis. Alternate translation: [Certainly]
Here, **Israel** represents the Israelite people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to the people of Israel]

Here the psalmist speaks of the **heart** of righteous people as **pure** and not blemished by wrong and sinful thoughts in contrast to having a **heart** that is impure because of sinful thoughts and motives and therefore morally dirty. What the psalmist means by **pure** here is that the person’s **heart** is “morally pure.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly or use an equivalent expression. Alternate translation: [to the ones who think about and want what is pleasing to God] or [to those with a morally pure heart]

In Jewish culture people considered the **heart** to be the center of a persons thoughts and feelings and here, the **heart** represents the intentions, thoughts and desires of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to those who think about and want what is pure] or [to those with a pure mind] or [to those with pure thoughts]

2.q: כִּ֭⁠מְעַט נטוי רַגְלָ֑⁠י כְּ֝⁠אַ֗יִן שפכה אֲשֻׁרָֽ⁠י
2.note: Here, **my feet** and **my steps** represent the Psalmist himself and the phrases **slipped** and **slide out** refer to abandoning doing what pleases God and instead choosing to sin. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the meaning with an equivalent expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I was tempted to stop obeying God. It was as if my feet almost slipped and as if my steps were almost caused to slide out from under me] or [I almost stopped trusting in God; I was almost guilty of sinning against him]

2.q: כִּ֭⁠מְעַט נטוי רַגְלָ֑⁠י כְּ֝⁠אַ֗יִן שפכה אֲשֻׁרָֽ⁠י
2.note: The phrases **my feet almost slipped** and **my steps almost were caused to slide out from under me** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine the phrases and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [my feet almost slipped] or [my feet almost slid out from under me]

The expression **my steps almost were caused to slide out** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you must state who did the action, the following verse implies that the Psalmist caused his own steps to almost slide out from under him when he looked at the “prosperity of the wicked” and did not also immediately go into “God’s sanctuary” so that he could “understand” the final “fate” of the wicked (see Psalm 73:17). Alternate translation: [I almost caused my steps to slide out from under me]

3.note: Here the word **because** indicates that what follows it in this verse is the reason for what precedes it in 73:2. Use a natural form for indicating this relationship. Alternate translation: [for]

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [when I saw the prosperity of the wicked, I was envious of the arrogant]

The Psalmist is using the adjectives **arrogant** and **wicked** as nouns in order to describe certain people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you could translate these words with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [of arrogant people when I saw the prosperity of wicked people] or [of the people who are arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the people who are wicked]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **prosperity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [when I saw how prosperous the wicked were]

4.note: The word the ULT translates as **ropes** refers to ropes or bonds that constrain a person. Here the psalmist is speaking of struggles or pains as if they were **ropes** or “bonds.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the meaning with an equivalent expression, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [struggles] or [emotional pains] or [pains]

The word the ULT translates as **until their death** could refer to: (1) the time before the death of wicked people in which case you can use the ULT as a model, or (2) the time at which wicked people die. Alternate translation: [in their death] or [at their death]

5.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **trouble**, you could express the same idea with a verb or in some other way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [They do not have to experience difficult things like the rest of man] or [They do not suffer the way other men do]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [people, and with people they are not afflicted] or [other people, and they are not afflicted like everyone else]

The expression **they are not afflicted** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you must state who did the action, the context implies that God did it. Alternate translation: [and God does not afflict them like he does the rest of man] or [and God does not afflict them like he does everyone else]

6.note: Here, the word **Therefore** introduces the result of 73:4–5. You can use a natural word or phrase in your language to express this relationship. Alternate translation: [As a result]

The psalmist is speaking of **pride** as if it were a **necklace** that wicked people wear around their neck. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparison, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they wear pride like a necklace] or [pride is like a necklace which they flaunt]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **pride**, you could express the same idea in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [they act pridefully for all to see, like someone who wears a necklace that they want everyone to see] or [they unashamedly act proud in front of everyone, like a person wearing a necklace that they want everyone to see]

A **necklace** is a type of jewelry worn around the neck in order to adorn the body and make a person look more attractive. If your readers would not be familiar with necklaces, you could use the name of something similar that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternately, if you are using footnotes, you could make a footnote explaining what a **necklace** is. Alternate translation: [a neck ornament for them]

The psalmist is speaking of **violence** as it were a **garment** that people wear. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the meaning with a comparable expression, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [violence covers them like a garment] or [violence covers them like clothing]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **violence**, you could express the same idea in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [they are proud of their violent actions and display them openly, as a person who wears a garment for all to see]

7.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **imaginations**, you could express the same idea in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [they are constantly imagining evil things in their hearts] or [they are constantly thinking about evil things in their hearts]

Here the psalmist speaks of the **heart** of a wicked person as if it were a container that could overflow with evil **imaginations** (thoughts). If it would be helpful to your readers, you could express the meaning using an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [their heart is constantly thinking of evil things to do] or [their heart is constantly imagining evil thoughts]

The psalmist is describing the mind of wicked people by association with their **heart**, which is where a person’s thoughts and intentions were viewed as coming from in Jewish culture. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [they constantly think of evil things to do] or [the imaginations of their inner being overflow]

8.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the ideas of **evil** and **oppression**, you could express the same ideas in some other way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and wickedly speak about oppressing people]

The phrase **they speak from an elevated place** means “they speak arrogantly.” If it would be helpful to your readers, you could indicate that explicitly. Alternate translation: [they speak arrogantly]

9.note: Here, **mouth** and **tongue** represents “speech.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [They talk as if they are God who is in the heavens, and their speech goes through the earth]

The word translated as **in the heavens** could be translated as: (1) **in the heavens** as modeled by the ULT in which case the psalmist is describing the role or authority of God by association with the **heavens**, Alternate translation: [They talk with their mouth as if they are God who is in heaven] or [They talk as if they are in the position of God] or (2) “against the heavens” in which case the psalmist is describing God by association with the **heavens**. Alternate translation: [They set their mouth against the heavens] or [They set their mouth against God]

The psalmist is speaking of the **tongue** (words or speech) of wicked people as if it could go **through the earth**. What he means is that these wicked people go about talking wickedly (and bragging) as they live their daily lives on earth and proudly act as if they are not accountable to God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they constantly talk wickedly as if they rule the earth] or [and they walk about talking wickedly]

10.note: The term translated as **Therefore** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [This is why]
This could mean: (1) “God’s people love the wicked people” or (2) “the wicked people return to this place”

The expression **are drained** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you must state who did the action, the context implies that people did it. Alternate translation: [and they drain the waters of a full cup]

The psalmist is speaking of listening to words as if they were drinking **water** out of a cup. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the meaning with a simile or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and believe all that they say]
This could mean: (1) “God’s people listen gladly to the words of the wicked people” or (2) “the wicked people have plenty of food to eat and wine to drink”

11.note: The phrases **How does God know** and **is there knowledge in the Most High** mean basically the same thing. The second phrase emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and it would be good to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation rather than combining them. However, if it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine the phrases into one. Alternate translation: [How could God know?] or [Does God have knowledge?]

Here the word **they** could refer to: (1) wicked people. Alternate translation: [And those who are wicked say] or [And the wicked say] or (2) people who are righteous and obey God. Alternate translation: [And righteous people say] or [And godly people say]

Here wicked people are not asking for information but are using the question form to express that they do not think God knows or cares about the evil things they do. If you would not use the question form for this purpose in your language, you could translate these questions as statements or exclamations and communicate the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [Surely God does not know what we are doing! Surely the Most High has no knowledge of it!] or [Surely God does not care about we are doing! Surely what we are doing does not matter to the Most High!]
This portion of this verse is a quotation of what the wicked people said or thought to themselves. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language.

12.note: The psalmist is using the term **Behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [See]

The Psalmist is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun in order to describe a group of people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you could translate this word with an equivalent phrase. See how you translated the phrase **the wicked** in 73:3. Alternate translation: [wicked ones]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **ease**, you could express the same idea in some other way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [they are always comfortable] or [they are always carefree]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **wealth**, you could express the same idea in some other way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [they become increasingly wealthy]

13.note: Here the psalmist uses the word **Surely** to emphasize his strong thoughts and feelings about the certainty of what he states in this verse. Use a natural form in your language for expressing this emphasis. Alternate translation: [Certainly]

The psalmist is describing his thoughts and intentions by association with his **heart**, which Jews viewed as the center of a person’s thoughts and intentions. The expression **I have kept my heart clean** means he has intentionally kept his thoughts and intentions morally pure (free from sin). You may have an equivalent expression in your language, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I have kept my thoughts pure]

The psalmist is describing his actions by association with his **hands**, which he would use to do the actions. The psalmist is using the symbolic action of hand washing to declare his **innocence**. In that culture hand washing was a common practice that people did to publicly assert that they were innocent. (See Deuteronomy 21:6 and Matthew 27:24.) Here the psalmist is saying that he has **washed** his **hands in innocence** as a way to declare that he is guiltless. See how you translated the similar phrase in Psalm 26:6. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and kept my actions pure to show that I am innocent] or [and kept my actions free from sin]

14.note: The expression **I have been stricken … and punished** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [For you have stricken me all of the day and punished me every morning] or [For you have afflicted me all of the day and punished me every morning]

The phrase **all of the day** is a common expression meaning “every day” or “constantly.” If this phrase does not have this meaning in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [constantly]

15.q: אִם־אָ֭מַרְתִּי אֲסַפְּרָ֥ה כְמ֑וֹ הִנֵּ֤ה ד֭וֹר בָּנֶ֣י⁠ךָ בָגָֽדְתִּי
15.note: The psalmist is describing a hypothetical situation in order to tell his readers what would have happened if he had said the things he was thinking out loud. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a situation that could happen. Alternate translation: [If I had said, ‘I will recount such things,’ then I would have betrayed the generation of your children.]
The psalmist is using the term **behold** to emphasize what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [certainly]

The psalmist is speaking of God’s people, his spiritual children, as if they were his biological **children**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your followers] or [the people who obey you]

16.note: Here the author’s **eyes** represent his evaluation or estimation as he tried to understand why wicked people seemed to prosper and he suffered. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to me] or [to think about]

17.note: Here the plural word **sanctuaries** could: (1) refer to the Jerusalem temple, in which case the plural is intensifying the meaning. Alternate translation: [the great sanctuary of God] or [the great temple of God] (2) refer to the precincts of the Jerusalem temple. Alternate translation: [the precincts of the temple of God] or [the precincts of God’s temple]
Alternate translation: [then I understood their fate] or [then I understood what will happen to those who are wicked]

18.note: See how you translated the word **Surely** in 73:1 where it is used with the same meaning.

The psalmist is speaking of the fact that God does not allow wicked people to have a secure future as if God had **set them in slippery places**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you do not give them a good future]

Here the word **you** refers to God and the word **them** refers to wicked people. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could indicate that explicitly. Alternate translation: [Surely you, God, set wicked people in slippery places]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **destruction**, you could express the same idea in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [you cause them to be destroyed]

19.note: The psalmist is using the term **How** to focus attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you could use in your translation.

The expression **they are brought** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you must state who did the action, the context implies that “God” does it. Alternate translation: [God brings them]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **desolation**, you could express the same idea in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [God will destroy them as in a moment] or [they will be suddenly destroyed]
The phrase **as in a moment** means “suddenly” or “all at once.” If it would be helpful to your readers, you could indicate that explicitly. Alternate translation: [all at once]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The psalmist is using the phrases **They come to an end** and **they perish** together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [They come to an end] or [They perish]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **terrors**, you could express the same idea in another way that is natural in your language.

20.q: כַּ⁠חֲל֥וֹם מֵ⁠הָקִ֑יץ אֲ֝דֹנָ⁠י בָּ⁠עִ֤יר ׀ צַלְמָ֬⁠ם תִּבְזֶֽה
20.note: The psalmist is comparing the short and temporary duration of a **dream**, which is over after a person **awakes**, to the fact that God will **despise** wicked people when he rouses himself to action and judges them. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the basis of this comparison or express this meaning in plain language. Alternate translation: [They will disappear as quickly as a dream disappears when a person awakes in the morning; Lord, when you act, you will cause them to disappear]

21.note: The phrases **When my heart was embittered** and **I was pierced in my kidneys** mean basically the same thing. The second phrase emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and it would be good to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation rather than combining them. However, if it would be helpful to your readers, you could connect the phrases with a word other than **and** in order to show that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [When my heart was embittered, yes, when I was pierced in my kidneys]

The psalmist is describing his inner being and thoughts by association with his **heart**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I was embittered] or [I was embittered within]
The psalmist is describing his feelings by association with his **kidneys**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language as modeled by the UST.

22.note: The phrase **I was not knowing** means “I was without knowledge” or “I was ignorant.” If it would be helpful to your readers, you could indicate that explicitly. Alternate translation: [and I was without knowledge] or [and I was ignorant]

The psalmist is speaking of his prior **stupid** and ignorant thinking and action toward God as if he had been behaving like an **animal**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the meaning with a comparison, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I acted like an animal toward you] or [I acted and thought like an animal before you] or [I acted like a fool toward you]
Here the word **you** refers to God. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could indicate that explicitly. Alternate translation: [with you, God]

23.note: The psalmist is speaking of God’s continual presence with him as if God were continually holding his **right hand**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the meaning with a comparison, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you are constantly with me] or [you are constantly with me. It is as if you are holding me by my right hand]

24.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **counsel**, you could express the same idea in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [You guide me by teaching me instructive things] or [You guide me by teaching me]

Here the term **glory** could refer to: (1) God’s presence in this life or after death. Alternate translation: [and afterward you will take me into your glorious presence] or [and after I die you will take me into your presence] (2) the glory or honor that God would give the psalmist in this life or after death because he had remained faithful and lived a righteous life. Alternate translation: [and afterward you will receive me with honor] or [and when I die you will receive me with honor] or [and at the end of my life you will receive me and honor me]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **glory**, you could express the same idea in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and afterward you will take me into your glorious presence] or [and afterward you will honor me when you receive me]

25.note: Here psalmist is implying the words “but you?” If it would be helpful to your readers, you could indicate that explicitly as modeled by the ULT. Alternate translation: [Whom have I in heaven but you?]

The psalmist is not asking for information but is using the question form for emphasis. If you would not use a rhetorical question for this purpose in your language, you could translate these words as a statement or an exclamation and communicate the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [There is no one I have in heaven but you!]
Alternate translation: [And with you I desire nothing on the earth]

26.note: The psalmist is referring to his entire body as if it were his **flesh**, and he is referring to his mind and/or spirit as if they were his **heart**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly or use an equivalent expression. Alternate translation: [I may become physically and emotionally weak] or [My body and my mind may fail] or [My body and my spirit may fail]

26.q: כָּלָ֥ה שְׁאֵרִ֗⁠י וּ⁠לְבָ֫בִ֥⁠י צוּר־לְבָבִ֥⁠י וְ⁠חֶלְקִ֗⁠י אֱלֹהִ֥ים לְ⁠עוֹלָֽם
26.note: Alternate translation: [My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart forever]

The psalmist is speaking of **God** as if he were a **rock**. The term **rock** is associated with strength so by calling God **the rock of my heart**, he means that God is the strength of his heart. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the meaning with a comparison, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [but God, you are like a rock for my heart, and you are my portion forever] or [but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever]

27.note: The psalmist is using the term **behold** to bring attention to and emphasize the certainty of what he is about to say. Use a word or phrase that would communicate that meaning in your language. Alternate translation: [indeed]
Alternate translation: [you will destroy everyone who is unfaithful to you]

28.note: Alternate translation: [But for me, God’s companionship is my greatest good] or [But for me, God’s presence is my good]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **closeness**, you could express the same idea in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [being close to God is good for me] or [being near to God is good for me]

The psalmist speaks of **Yahweh** as if he were a physical place that a person could go to for **refuge**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the meaning with a comparison, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Like a person runs to a shelter to keep them safe when they are in danger, so I have chosen to trust you to keep me safe]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **refuge**, you could express the same idea in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I trust the Lord, Yahweh, to protect me]

The phrase **in order to** marks **recount all your works** as the goal or purpose for which the psalmist **made the Lord, Yahweh** his **refuge**. Use a natural way in your language for indicating that this is the goal or purpose.
Alternate translation: [that I might make known to people all your works] or [that I may declare all your deeds]
